title: Fake Anthropic AI previews lure in overeager employees
summary: Everyone wants to know what Anthropic is up to, and hackers are gleefully exploiting the fact. New research from cybersecurity company Cofense describes a phishing campaign that hooks overeager enterprise users by making them think they are getting an invite to a private invite-only Anthropic preview. In reality, adversarial actors are trying to steal Google and Microsoft login credentials, exploiting video teleconferencing software GoTo Webinar branding to do so. “It sells exclusivity,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “Fear of missing out is the oldest lure in the book.” Every organization is trying to figure out where AI fits, he noted, and a private preview of Anthropic’s newest technology is exactly the invitation an ambitious employee would want to accept. “The attackers did not pick Anthropic at random,” he said. “They picked whatever is hottest in the news cycle. Next month, it may be another name.” How attackers lure users with spoofed Anthropic invites GoTo Webinar is a widely used platform, and its meeting invitation emails are typically not blocked by security tools . The Cofense researchers found that attackers are exploiting this fact by sending what seems to be an invitation email from a legitimate sender; when users click on the link to register for the fake webinar, they are instead sent to a compromised URL. The email offers what the researchers call a “tantalizing” offer: “This private, invitation-only virtual session brings together a select group of participants to a focused conversation on AI systems, research, and the future of frontier models,” it reads. A URL shortener circumvents email security tools, and the attackers use subdomains and dashes (-) to hide the malicious URL. The link itself appears to have been generated by Zapier, a legitimate company whose tools are designed to work with Claude, ChatGPT, and other AI compatible with Model Context Protocol (MCP). The email sender address appears to be customercare@gotowebinar[.]com

title: Apple brings touch to the Mac with $2,899 OLED MacBook Pro
summary: Following the release of the new 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro earlier this week, Apple has bought the “touch experience” to its professional laptop series, introducing a $2,899 (and up) MacBook Pro you can use with touch. It’s very fast, very thin, very light, with an impressive PROLED XDR display and up to 24 hours battery life. A brief tour through the key specs Very fast: Available in 14- and 16-inch models, the new MacBook Pro uses Apple’s powerful M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. They support up to 64GB of unified memory (128GB on M5 Max) and up to 16TB of storage. Apple says the M5 Max can run LLMs with hundreds of billions of parameters entirely on-device. Very thin: The 14-inch model is 0.59 inch (1.50 cm) thick, while the 16-inch is 0.63 inch (1.60 cm), so these are only a little thicker than a MacBook Air. Apple says the thinner design is a benefit of the move to an OLED display. Very light: The 14-inch weighs 3 pounds, half a pound less than the non-touch equivalent MacBook Pro. The 16-inch weighs 4 pounds, which is 0.7 pounds lighter. Industry-leading PROLED XDR display: A tandem OLED panel with up to 2,000 nits peak brightness (1,000 nits sustained brightness) for both HDR and SDR, and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. Refresh rate is variable from 10Hz up to 120Hz. Up to 24 hours of battery life: Apple says this is the maximum and that battery life varies by use and configuration. It also varies by model — the 14-inch yields “just” 22 hours battery life. Fast charging takes the battery to 50% in 30 minutes. Unpacking those numbers, it’s crystal-clear Apple has not stinted on the performance of this pro Mac, with a price tag to match. IDC data shows that 66% of all touch notebooks are purchased by enterprises. This is a form factor bought for flexibility for field workers, educators, and professionals who move between typing, tapping, and handwriting. Touch on a Mac Which brings me to the “touch experience.” Apple hasn’t replaced the traditional Mac interface with touch

title: Anthropic and OpenAI diverge on who should pull the plug on risky AI
summary: OpenAI and Anthropic agree that frontier AI systems need stronger oversight, but they are proposing sharply different approaches to stopping models that pose serious risks: Anthropic wants courts empowered to suspend dangerous systems, while OpenAI argues developers should be required to maintain and use effective shutdown controls. The proposals appear in separate submissions to California Governor Gavin Newsom following his September 18 executive order directing state officials to consider additional safeguards for frontier AI systems. Both companies support independent safety assessments and expanded reporting of incidents involving AI systems that act beyond their intended permissions. “If the AG concludes, informed by the independent evaluation, that a frontier AI company’s models pose a near-term risk of catastrophic harm, they should be able to seek a court order to suspend a model’s deployment, internal use, or further development,” Anthropic wrote in its October 15 submission. OpenAI, in its October 20 letter , called for an amendment to California’s Senate Bill 53 (SB 53). “We support amending SB 53 to require frontier developers to maintain effective shutdown controls and an enforceable duty to use them when unsafe conditions arise, and no lesser intervention would adequately address the risk,” OpenAI wrote. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said the two approaches address complementary needs. “The operator must contain the unsafe activity promptly. Independent review must examine both intervention and inaction,” he said. Newsom’s executive order , N-9-26, directs California’s Government Operations Agency, in consultation with the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services and national experts, to submit recommendations by November 16 on potential amendments to existing AI safety laws. title: What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?
summary: Using AI for roles from executive assistants to chiefs of staff, companies are boasting about doing more with less, creating tension with their human workers On an average workday, Dhruv Amin chats with dozens of colleagues to get things done at his AI startup Anything. He might ask Gwen, his executive assistant, to schedule a meeting, then troubleshoot a technical problem with Cody, his coding partner. Then he might check in with Betsy for search engine optimization, or Juno for onboarding customers. If the office runs out of snacks, he sends a Slack message to Justin, the office manager charged with stocking the kitchen. But none of these co-workers are people. They’re artificial intelligence agents, software that handles tasks without human intervention. Anything is one of several startups building them, and betting on a future where workplaces will increasingly turn over their sales, marketing, coding and other tasks to semi-autonomous AI. title: Simplifying .NET toolchain installs with dotnetup
summary: If you’ve experimented with Rust , you already know how simple it is to get a basic toolchain in place, with the simple rustup command-line tool. The same tool works on Windows, macOS, and Linux, building a consistent environment that’s ready for you to pick up your favorite coding editor and start work. It’s a simple enough tool, and one that’s done much to help popularize a new programming language. With rustup, you know what you’re getting, and you can start working on any laptop, anywhere. Managing .NET environments is complex Things are not so simple with .NET. Yes, it’s cross platform, running on Windows, macOS, and Linux. However, it’s not so easy to set up, often relying on third-party repositories and installers, as well as many different scripts that install different versions and their associated platforms. Have you installed ASP.NET Core? Do you need Aspire, or are you building a mobile application with MAUI? Everything has its own custom install route, which will likely differ depending on the target OS. To cap it off, .NET tools often need to be run with the highest level of privileges needed, requiring developers to have administrative rights. None of that is particularly developer friendly, and it makes it hard to build .NET tooling into ephemeral environments like CI/CD build tools and runners, where you need to populate a hosted container for test and compilation, loading a new instance of the .NET CLI every time you fire up a GitHub Action — and having to run tooling with a much higher set of privileges than you want for an automated process. Things get more confusing when you’re maintaining an application with a current build of .NET at the same time as updating it for the next long-term release, all on the same development workstation. With platform-specific toolchains and installation mechanisms, complexity gets in the way of coding and .NET becomes less of a priority, despite its cross-platform features and its maturity. title: AIに任せているのは「判断」ではなく、「判断材料づくり」である
summary: これまでの連載では、同じデータ、同じ定義を使うことの大切さを書いてきました。今回の話は、その延長にあります。AIが作る判断材料の質は、元のデータと、「何を異常と呼ぶか」という定義の質で決まります。データがばらばらで、定義が人によって違えば、AIは速く、大量に、間違った判断材料を作ります。どこまで任せるかを考える前に、判断材料の質を揃えておく必要があります。 ※第1回:「経営KGIと現場KPIをつなぐ」、第2回:「同じデータ・同じ定義」を誰がつくるのか、第3回:「同じ判断材料の共有」についてお話ししました。 「AIが判断したので」は会議で通るか 「それはAIが判断したことなので」。この言葉を、経営会議で口にできる人はいないはずです。 AIが賢くなるほど、「どこまで任せるか」は技術の問いではなく、経営の問いになります。今回は、弊社が製造業のお客様と取り組む中で見えてきた、「判断の仕分け」の考え方をお話しします。 結論を先に述べます。公開されている事例を見る限り、AIに任されているのは「判断」ではなく、「判断材料づくり」です。 判断を3つに分ける 「AIに任せるか」と問われると、判断を1つの塊として考えがちです。しかし判断は、少なくとも3つに分けられます（図１）。 判断材料づくり：見る、集める、整える、比べる 決める：選択肢から選び、結果に責任を負う 実行：決めたことを現場で行う 設備保全で言えば、センサーを見て異常を見つけ、マニュアルや過去の記録を集め、対策案を比べるのが材料づくりです。どの対策をいつ実施するかを決め、実際に作業するのが、その先の2つです。 図1．判断は3つに分けられる 判断材料づくりは、量が多く、速さが求められ、人には負担の重い仕事です。一方で「決める」には、結果への責任がついてきます。責任を負えるのは人だけです。ここに、仕分けの出発点があります。 4つの事例に見る共通点 弊社の公開事例を見ると、共通する構図があります。 弊社の公開事例 AIが担う部分（材料づくり） 人が決める部分 Georgia-Pacific社 150超の拠点で約85,000個の振動センサーを監視 異常予兆検出をするAIモデルは30,000個超 運転員・監督者が、修理を計画保全にまとめて日程を決める ロッキード・マーティン社 飛行データからの部品故障の予測 データ整形の約85%を自動化 SASとの協業では、症状データと整備記録から診断し、マニュアルの該当手順を参照元付きで提示する仕組みを検証 任務の中止は乗員、運航機と予備部品の選択は顧客、整備作業は整備士 Wienerberger社 分断データの統合 エネルギー消費の監視 洞察と推奨の生成 デジタルツインでの事前検証 現場知識を持つ技術者がモデルを改善し、変更は検証後に実施 SAS×NSW様のOEE改善デモ 経営KGI、現場KPIダッシュボード 異常予兆検出のしきい値の自動設定 要因候補のパラメータ表示 生成AIによる対策案の提示 対応方法の決定 何をAIに任せてよいか：2つの軸 では、どの判断ならAIに任せてよいのでしょうか。2つの軸で考えます。 1つ目は、判断の基準がどこまで明文化されているかです。「この値を一定回数続けて超えたら異常」と言えるなら、機械に任せられます。弊社の事例でも、異常を知らせるしきい値は、担当者の経験則ではなく、統計の考え方（管理図）で自動的に設定し、基準を標準化しています。基準は人が決め、適用は機械が行う。この分担です。 2つ目は、間違えたときの影響と、元に戻せるかです。データ整形や異常アラートは、間違えても戻せます。任務の中止や部品の交換は、戻せません。 図2．基準の明文化度 × 誤りの影響 この2軸で、4つの領域に分かれます。 基準が明確で影響が小さければ、AIに任せる。 [...] The post AIに任せているのは「判断」ではなく、「判断材料づくり」である appeared first on SAS Blogs .

title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
summary: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. title: SaaS is dead?
summary: In this solo episode, I explain why I say SaaS is dead and what I see taking its place. For 15 years, SaaS meant paying engineers to build a tool and charging per seat, and now models like Opus 5.5, GPT-6, and Argon make the tool easy to build. I walk through what I call smart SaaS: give the tool away for free, collect data and network effects, and make money by upselling AI agents and human services. I share a calorie tracking example, three ways to charge, and why enterprises still pay per seat. If you build software, this episode gives you a map for building something people want in a market where the tool is free.
